Day 5 — Supervised Learning.Regularization&Trees
These are the exercises for one teaching day of Module 3 of the Health Data Science MSc. Each chapter is one exercise you can finish in a single sitting, with an R path and a Python path doing the same work. Pick one; in class we go through R most of the time.

title: Exercise 5.1 — Evaluating a regression model on training and test data
text:
Stretch
On Day 3 you fitted a straight line to predict glucose and measured its error with a loss function. A model is only useful if it also predicts people it has not seen. In this exercise we fit a model on the training rows, predict both the training and the test rows, and compare the errors. The comparison tells us whether the model is overfitting (much better on training than on test) or underfitting (similar on both, but poor on both).
Suppose we believe that the relationship between glucose and age is not a straight line but a cubic:
\[\widehat{\text{glucose}} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{age} + \beta_2\,\text{age}^2 + \beta_3\,\text{age}^3\]
Theory: polynomial features as a pre-processing step; recipes, workflows and pipelines; predictions on training and test data; mean squared error, root mean squared error and mean absolute error; overfitting and underfitting.

title: Reading — Lasso and ridge in a picture
text:
The two penalties
This page has no code to write. Read it before Exercise 5.2. It explains one picture that you will meet in almost every textbook on regularisation, and it shows why the lasso can set a coefficient to exactly zero while ridge cannot.
An ordinary linear regression chooses the coefficients that give the lowest training MSE. Lasso and ridge add a price for large coefficients. With two predictors, they choose the pair \((\beta_1, \beta_2)\) that minimises
\[\text{Lasso:}\quad \text{MSE} + \lambda\,\big(|\beta_1| + |\beta_2|\big)
\qquad\qquad
\text{Ridge:}\quad \text{MSE} + \lambda \times \tfrac{1}{2}\big(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2\big)\]
You choose \(\lambda\). With \(\lambda = 0\) there is no price, and you get the ordinary fit, written \(\hat\beta\). The larger \(\lambda\) is, the more the coefficients are pulled towards zero.
crumbs: 2  Reading — Lasso and ridge in a picture

title: Reading — Lasso and ridge in a picture
text:
The picture
Each point of the plane below is one possible pair \((\beta_1, \beta_2)\).

The black dot \(\hat\beta\) is the ordinary fit: the pair with the lowest training MSE.
The red curves are contours of the training MSE, like the contour lines of a map. Every pair on one curve has the same MSE, and the MSE grows as you move outwards from \(\hat\beta\). They are ellipses here because the two predictors are correlated.
The blue shape holds every pair whose penalty is no more than a budget \(s\). For the lasso, \(|\beta_1| + |\beta_2| \le s\) is a diamond. For ridge, \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2 \le s^2\) is a circle.
The white dot is the fitted model: the first point where a red curve, growing outwards from \(\hat\beta\), touches the blue shape.










The fitted model is the pair with the lowest MSE that stays within the budget. On the left, the first touch is at the top corner of the diamond, so \(\beta_1 = 0\): the lasso has dropped the first predictor. On the right, the circle has no corners, and the first touch is at a point where both coefficients are smaller than in \(\hat\beta\) but neither is zero.
The penalty \(\lambda\) and the budget \(s\) are two descriptions of the same fit. We choose \(\lambda\) and fit the model. Adding up the absolute values of the fitted coefficients then gives \(s\), which tells us how big to draw the diamond. The worked example below does exactly that.
crumbs: 2  Reading — Lasso and ridge in a picture

Every column averages 0, so the model needs no intercept: \(\hat y = \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2\). The ordinary fit is \((3, 1)\), which predicts all four \(y\) values exactly, so its MSE is 0.

Step 1 — The red contours
For any pair \((\beta_1, \beta_2)\), predict the four \(y\) values and average the squared residuals. With these data, the calculation simplifies to
\[\text{MSE} = (3 - \beta_1)^2 + (1 - \beta_2)^2 .\]
So in this example the red contours are circles centred at \((3, 1)\). The farther out we go, the higher the training MSE. (They are circles rather than ellipses because \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are uncorrelated here.)


Step 2 — Choose \(\lambda\) and fit the lasso
Set \(\lambda = 2\). The lasso chooses the pair that minimises training MSE plus \(2 \times\) the sum of the absolute coefficients. Here is how a few candidate pairs compare.

Take the move from \((2, 1)\) to \((2, 0)\). Setting \(\beta_2\) to zero increases the training MSE by 1 but saves 2 in penalty, so the total drops from 7 to 6. Moving farther towards zero, to \((1, 0)\), increases the MSE by 3 and saves only 2, so the total goes back up.


Step 3 — Draw the diamond from the fitted coefficients
The winner, \((2, 0)\), uses a budget of \(s = |2| + |0| = 2\). Draw the diamond holding all pairs whose absolute coefficients add up to at most 2. Its four corners are \((2, 0)\), \((0, 2)\), \((-2, 0)\) and \((0, -2)\).









Now picture a red circle growing outwards from \((3, 1)\). The first touch is at \((2, 0)\), the right-hand corner of the diamond. Why? If a point inside the diamond had a lower MSE, it would also have an equal or smaller penalty, and so it would have beaten \((2, 0)\) in the lasso fit.

At \(\lambda = 4\), the move from \((2, 0)\) to \((1, 0)\) still increases the MSE by 3, but now it saves 4 in penalty. That is why the stronger penalty favours the smaller coefficient and gives a smaller diamond.









Read the panels in order. \(\beta_2\) reaches zero first, at \(\lambda = 2\), and \(\beta_1\) follows at \(\lambda = 6\). At \(\lambda = 0\) there is no penalty, and the diamond simply passes through the ordinary fit. The lasso has dropped the weaker predictor first. With many predictors, this is how the lasso selects variables.

The lasso’s winner, \((2, 0)\), loses under ridge. Ridge prefers \((1.5, 0.5)\), which keeps both coefficients. Squaring makes small coefficients very cheap: a coefficient of 0.5 adds only \(0.5^2 = 0.25\) before \(\lambda\) is applied, so there is little to gain by pushing it all the way to zero.









Turning up \(\lambda\) shrinks the ridge circle, but the fit never lands on an axis:

In this tidy example, with uncorrelated predictors, there is a simple pattern. Ridge divides both coefficients by the same number, \(1 + \lambda/2\), so they get smaller but never reach zero. The lasso subtracts the same amount, \(\lambda/2\), from each coefficient’s size and stops at zero, so the smaller coefficient reaches zero first. With correlated predictors the arithmetic is messier, but the pictures tell the same story.

title: Reading — Lasso and ridge in a picture
text:
Why the corners matter
The diamond’s corners lie on the axes, and every point on an axis has one coefficient equal to zero. A red contour arriving from many directions meets a corner before it meets an edge. A circle has no corners, so a first touch exactly on an axis would be a coincidence. With ten predictors the diamond becomes a shape in ten dimensions with many corners and edges, each one a place where some of the coefficients are exactly zero. That is why the lasso often keeps only a handful of predictors, while ridge keeps them all.
crumbs: 2  Reading — Lasso and ridge in a picture

title: Reading — Lasso and ridge in a picture
text:
Before you start Exercise 5.2

Standardise first. The penalty treats every coefficient alike. A coefficient for age per year is ten times smaller than the same coefficient for age per decade, so without standardising, the penalty would depend on the units you happened to choose.
Choosing \(\lambda\). In Exercise 5.2 you will try several values of \(\lambda\) and keep the one that predicts best on rows the model was not fitted on. Each value is one picture like the ones above: the larger \(\lambda\), the smaller the shape, and the fewer columns the lasso keeps.







TipKey points




Lasso and ridge minimise the training misfit plus \(\lambda\) times a penalty on the coefficients.
Each fit can be drawn as the first touch between the misfit contours and a budget shape: a diamond for the lasso, a circle for ridge.
The diamond has corners on the axes, so the lasso can set coefficients exactly to zero and select predictors. Ridge shrinks every coefficient and drops none.
A larger \(\lambda\) means a smaller budget \(s\), and so a smaller shape.

title: Exercise 5.2 — Hyperparameters: choosing the lasso and ridge penalty
text:
Stretch
Some settings of a model are not learnt from the data: we choose them before fitting. They are called hyperparameters. In this exercise the hyperparameters are those of regularisation: a linear regression that pays a price for large coefficients, so that it fits the training rows a little less closely in exchange for a simpler model. How large the price is, \(\lambda\), must be chosen, and we choose it by trying several values and keeping the one that predicts best on rows the model has not seen. The page Lasso and ridge in a picture explains what the penalty does.
Theory: hyperparameters; a validation set; the lasso and ridge penalties; grid search, random search and zooming in; refitting the chosen model and checking it once on the test rows.

title: Exercise 5.3 — Evaluating a classification model on training and test data
text:
Stretch
Exercise 5.1 evaluated a regression model by the size of its errors. A classification model predicts a class, diabetes or no diabetes, so an error is simply a wrong class, and there are two kinds of wrong. In this exercise we fit a logistic regression on the training rows, turn its probabilities into classes with a threshold, and measure its performance on the training and the test rows, first with metrics that depend on the threshold and then with the ROC curve and the AUC, which do not. Finally we add more predictors and compare.
Theory: predicted probabilities and predicted classes; accuracy, precision, recall, sensitivity and specificity; which class is the event; the distribution of predicted probabilities; the ROC curve and the area under it (AUC); underfitting in classification.

title: Exercise 5.3 — Evaluating a classification model on training and test data
text:
NoteStretch — the threshold for the richer model



Suppose a missed case costs five times as much as an unnecessary test, so a threshold costs 5 × (false negatives) + 1 × (false positives). Work that out for thresholds 0.1 to 0.9 on the test rows, for the age-only model and for the five-predictor model: which threshold is cheapest for each, and how much cheaper is the richer model at its best threshold?

title: Exercise 5.4 — Decision trees, overfitting and tuning
text:
Stretch
A decision tree classifies a person by asking a sequence of yes-or-no questions: is glucose above 128? If so, is body mass above 30? Each answer sends the person down one branch, until they reach a leaf, which gives a predicted class and a probability. Trees are easy to read, and they can model interactions and non-linear effects without being told to. Their weakness is that a tree can keep splitting until it has memorised the training rows. In this exercise we fit a tree, watch it overfit, restrain it by hand, and then let a grid search choose the restraint for us.
Theory: splits, nodes and leaves; tree depth and minimum node size as hyperparameters; overfitting in trees; grid search with cross-validation; the test set is used once, at the end.
crumbs: 5  Exercise 5.4 — Decision trees, overfitting and tuning

Leave tree_depth and min_n at their defaults and tune cost_complexity instead (in Python, ccp_alpha), over the values 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01 and 0.1. Which value is chosen, how many leaves has the tuned tree, and how does its test AUC compare with the tree tuned above?

title: Exercise 5.5 — Random forests and tuning with a workflow
text:
Stretch
A single decision tree is easy to read but unstable: a few different people in the training rows can give a very different tree, and a deep tree overfits. A random forest grows hundreds of trees, each on a different bootstrap sample of the training rows and each allowed to look at only a random subset of the predictors at every split, and averages their votes. The averaging cancels much of the noise that each single tree has memorised.
Goal. In this exercise you will:
Theory: bagging and random predictor subsets; the hyperparameters mtry and min_n; grid search with cross-validation; finalising a tuned model; why a forest’s training performance says little.
crumbs: 6  Exercise 5.5 — Random forests and tuning with a workflow
